components.text: Whether first-person experiential access is incompatible with physical identity.
It contacts the demand that physicalism explain privileged first-person access to qualitative experience.
Whether failure of lower-scale definition requires a nonphysical ontology.
It replaces microphysical definability with natural explanation at the scale where qualitative properties occur.
Whether Mary's epistemic gain is merely occupation-dependent acquaintance or ability.
It directly disputes that Mary's novelty is exhausted by ability or state acquaintance.
It supplies a determinate qualitative fact but does not directly refute the scale-specific naturalist classification of that fact.
Whether autonomous natural properties can accommodate mentality without another substance.
It challenges a naturalized example of aboutness by distinguishing intrinsic representation from observer-derived evidence.
Whether intentional attitudes require irreducible intrinsic mental aboutness.
It answers the aboutness challenge by invoking functionalist accounts of beliefs, desires, and intentional attitudes.
Whether physical causes can possess the reason-responsive content required for agency.
It contests the need for an extra substance by offering organism-level compatibilist conditions for free action.
Whether higher-level mental properties entail an additional mental substance.
It identifies that higher-scale or downward causation does not entail an additional substance bearing mental events.
Whether the two-way infinite-time premise required by the probability dilemma is credible.
Whether physical cosmology supplies recurrent conditions for later embodiment.
It rejects the dilemma's infinite-past premise by appealing to a finite-past, infinite-future cosmology.
Whether an infinite future generates recurrent physical conditions for persons.
It challenges the recurrence route by describing an expanding future in which complex conditions never return.
Whether acting from beliefs and desires supplies genuine reason-responsive freedom.
It disputes that action caused by physical beliefs and desires is sufficiently reason-responsive for genuine freedom.
It proposes higher-level mental causation but does not establish that its higher-level cause is an additional substance.
Whether infinite time and present existence support recurrence of the same person.
It challenges the personal-identity consequence by showing that recurrence alone does not identify a later animal as the same person.
The cross-species resemblance objection does not contact the separate reason-responsive causation argument.
Whether cross-species reincarnation must satisfy a qualitative-duplication condition.
Whether cosmological recurrence is necessary for later embodiment.
It replaces duplicate-based recurrence with persistence of one soul through embodiment in another organism.
It explains why cosmic recurrence is unnecessary but supplies no positive reembodiment mechanism beyond unknown conditions.
Whether the soul is an additional entity or the ordinary unified subject of experience.
It identifies the soul with the ordinary unified subject rather than positing a second rational subject.
Defining one current subject does not answer the cross-species persistence or resemblance condition.
Whether identity across embodiment requires qualitative resemblance to the present person.
It supplies a soul-based embodiment condition that does not require qualitative duplication across organisms.
It asserts preexisting souls but does not answer the demand for evidence of an additional nonphysical bearer.
It makes embodiment depend on suitable brains but does not answer whether future suitable organisms will exist.
Whether higher-scale brain events require a distinct nonphysical bearer.
It distinguishes continued existence of the subject from its ability to think or act without a functioning brain.
The dependence claim does not answer whether any later embodiment opportunity will occur.
Survival without activity does not supply identity conditions for later cross-species embodiment.
Whether pervasive brain dependence is compatible with an independently functioning soul.
Whether suitable brains merely enable capacities of an otherwise independent soul.
It presses the systematic dependence of human capacities on brain integrity against an independently functioning soul.
The evidence supports neural dependence but does not directly decide whether a nonoperative soul preexists or survives.
It bears on the subject's physical basis but does not analyze the unity-of-subject argument itself.
Whether soul attachment begins only when suitable neural organization exists.
It uses the absence of requisite fetal neural activity to challenge attachment of a soul before suitable brain organization.
The fetal onset evidence is relevant to dependence but does not directly address postmortem inactive survival.
